content: Flexion refers to a movement in which the angle between two bones at a joint decreases. This movement is facilitated by the coordinated action of the skeletal system (bones, cartilage, and ligaments) and the muscular system (muscles and tendons). For example, flexion occurs at the elbow joint when the hand is brought closer to the shoulder. Similarly, the trunk can be flexed toward the legs, or the neck can be flexed toward the chest. The opposite of flexion is extension, which increases the angle between the bones at a joint. Flexion typically occurs along the sagittal plane, meaning it involves forward and backward movements rather than side-to-side movements. Exercises Involving Flexion Active range of motion exercises often include flexion and extension movements. These exercises are commonly prescribed after an injury or surgery to restore mobility. Initially, they are performed under the guidance of a physical therapist or nurse, but patients may continue them independently as part of their rehabilitation. During the healing process, it is crucial to avoid forcing the limb into extreme flexion or extension, as this could cause further injury to the affected area. Muscles Involved in Flexion Upper Limb 1. Flexion of the Arm at the Shoulder Joint: The anterior compartment of the arm is responsible for this movement. Key muscles include: Coracobrachialis Biceps brachii 2. Flexion of the Forearm at the Elbow Joint: The anterior compartment of the arm contributes to this movement. Key muscles include: Biceps brachii Brachialis Brachioradialis The anterior compartment of the forearm also plays a role, with contributions from: Pronator teres Flexor carpi radialis Palmaris longus Flexor carpi ulnaris Flexor digitorum superficialis 3. Flexion of the Hand at the Wrist Joint: The anterior compartment of the forearm is involved. Key muscles include: Flexor carpi radialis Palmaris longus Flexor carpi ulnaris Flexor digitorum superficialis Flexor digitorum profundus 4. Flexion of the Proximal Phalanges at the Metacarpophalangeal Joint: Key muscles include: Lumbricals of the hand Dorsal interossei Palmar interossei Flexor digiti minimi brevis (specific to the little finger) 5. Flexion of the Intermediate Phalanges at the Proximal Interphalangeal Joints: Key muscle: Flexor digitorum superficialis 6. Flexion of the Distal Phalanges at the Distal Interphalangeal Joints: Key muscle: Flexor digitorum profundus 7. Flexion of the Thumb: Key muscles include: Flexor pollicis longus Flexor pollicis brevis Lower Limb 1. Flexion of the Femur/Thigh at the Hip Joint (L1-L2): Key muscles include: Iliopsoas Tensor fasciae latae Rectus femoris Additional minor contributions from other hip flexors 2. Flexion of the Leg at the Knee Joint (L5-S2): The posterior compartment of the thigh (hamstrings) is primarily responsible. Key muscles include: Biceps femoris Semitendinosus Semimembranosus Additional contributors include: Gracilis Sartorius Tensor fasciae latae Gastrocnemius Popliteus Plantaris (minor role) 3. Flexion of the Toes: The posterior compartment of the leg is involved. Key muscles include: Flexor hallucis longus Flexor digitorum longus Flexor digitorum brevis Quadratus plantae Flexor hallucis brevis Flexor digiti minimi brevis 4. Flexion of the Proximal Phalanges at the Metatarsophalangeal Joint: Key muscles include: Lumbrical muscles of the foot Plantar interossei Dorsal interossei Other Regions 1. Flexion of the Torso/Lumbar Vertebrae: Key muscle: Rectus abdominis 2. Flexion of the Neck at the Atlanto-Occipital Joint: Key muscle: Longus capitis
